summary: # CLO 2025 Academic Month Practical Course to Cultivate High-Quality 3D Talent ## Introduction Okay, my name is Kate Latham. I'm an assistant professor from Virginia Commonwealth University in Richmond, Virginia. With me is Christian Settle, a former student of mine, a recent graduate, and an independent contractor in 3D design. ## Program Overview A little bit about our department specifically: our current cohort is about this size currently. We have 200 merchandising students, 100 design students, and 97 merchandising minors. We also have two additional, including myself, so three total accredited academic CLO instructors. We are one of the first schools to begin implementing this new badge that CLO is giving out. Any student who graduates from the CLO course with an 86 average and above will receive this badge, which they can then share on LinkedIn and any platform that they need exposure. ## Importance of 3D Design I'd like to start off, before I explain the breakdown of the course that I teach, by talking a little bit about why students need to know about 3D, why it's so important, and why they should be prioritizing it in their lives. Everybody already knows the sustainability part; that's a given. It cuts down time and waste, cost, everything. But in addition to that, you sort of want some practical information to get them excited about this. Current assessments from various sources indicate that almost half of a survey of 60 luxury brands have claimed to begin incorporating technology like AR and VR into their marketing and other parts of their production. Additionally, a 30% rate of fashion brands have started implementing 3D processes in their production processes. Something really tangible for students to consider is that there are over 1,400 job listings currently related to 3D apparel design across four different platforms. In comparison, there are 2,100 estimated annual job openings in this field. That's a large percentage of those job openings, which is pretty encouraging and a really good reason to become proficient in 3D. ## Teaching Approach So, my teaching approach is as follows. It ultimately breaks down into what I call exercises in the classroom. This is a very structured step-by-step process where we go through specific tools and functions in the software. It's very criteria-based; we submit screenshots of the work at different stages for validation. ### Project-Based Learning We move into project-based learning, applying these tools and functions in a project setting. We also encourage the use of other software that can supplement CLO, such as Blender and Adobe programs like Illustrator and Photoshop, along with powerful programs like Unreal Engine. ### Course Breakdown The specific breakdown of what I focus on in my teaching starts with the interface and navigation. Students need to know how to get around the program first and foremost. Then we go into tools and focus on them in the order that they are relevant in a work process for a creative individual, specifically for fashion. We also focus on garment production; these tools will then feed into patterning and actually building the garment. Each garment will require different tools, know-hows, processes, and operations. Simultaneously, we develop our creative concepts for project-based learning, where students will begin to do research on target demographics, create personas, and build entire concepts to pull designs from. ### Advanced Techniques At the end of the course, we focus on advanced techniques, including high-quality renders of still shots and animation. We discuss motion files and again talk about those supplemental software programs, like Daz for creating custom avatars and Blender. ## Course Workflow The workflow of our four-month semester is broken down as follows: ### Month 1 In the first month, we go through approximately seven exercises. We have a discussion during these first two months, which roughly happens once a month. In these discussions, I like to talk about AI, ethics, and how we should be using AI and technologies that are now at our disposal as creatives. We also work on our personas or character profiles, depending on the final prompt we do for that semester. ### Month 2 In month two, we finish up our exercises—usually around 10 to 12 for the semester—and then we transition into a more creative phase. This is when students develop their entire collection, looking at trend research and pulling together design elements, finishings, and fabrication for the actual building of a collection. ### Exercise Examples Some examples of the exercises we do include: - **Elastic Properties and Wastepans:** Understanding how to manipulate these elements in design. - **The 3D Pen Tool:** This is particularly helpful for bodycon patterns, allowing students to create patterns by drawing on the avatar, which is a powerful tool for those who may not fully understand patterns. We also do custom fabric creation, asking students to create their own maps, including diffuse, normal, displacement, and opacity maps. ## Final Project The current final prompt for the semester is called "Designing for the Modern Professional." We aim to address the challenges faced by modern professionals who work long days and need wearability and comfort while prioritizing sustainability. The challenge we present is how to offer consumers multiple styles in a single garment. Students can choose between two focuses in the final stage: a digital direction or a fully digital route. - **Digital Direction:** This includes a five-look capsule collection. - **Fully Digital:** This involves a physical garment route and a heavier emphasis on video campaigns, animation rendering, line sheets, and lookbooks, potentially even a virtual showroom. ### Focus on Technology We also focus on tech packs, as they are very industry-relevant and necessary for any fashion endeavor. CLO can automatically generate these tech packs, making it easier for students. ## Example of Student Work Now, let me go into an example of student work, specifically Christian's project. For his final, students create a pitch deck for their entire concept and collection. Christian chose video games as his inspiration, creating a mood board centered around this theme. His project included a character profile that informed all design decisions, focusing on the concept, color palette, and fabrication for a lineup of five looks. One component of the final project is to print out full-scale patterns from CLO and create a physical garment from it. I emphasize that CLO isn't a magic tool for creating garments that are first-time-right samples. The mesh used in 3D design can be deceptive, and students need to train their eyes to recognize fit issues. ## Utilizing CLO There are three main uses of CLO that I recommend: 1. **Digitizing Slopers:** If your department has specific blocks or slopers, it is worthwhile to digitize them and use those exact slopers in CLO to work in tandem with real-world slopers. 2. **Exploring Historic Garments:** CLO provides a unique opportunity to explore and learn from iconic garments that students wouldn't otherwise have access to. 3. **Demonstrations:** CLO can serve as a valuable tool for demonstrations in other courses, particularly for complicated processes like tailoring. ## Challenges and Solutions CLO is a massive program and can be intimidating. Students often experience impostor syndrome, feeling as though they don’t belong. In my experience, it helps to constantly reiterate the core concepts and main functions, which are consistently found in the property editor or right-click pop-up menus. Students have expressed how beneficial written and video tutorials are, especially when they pertain directly to the material covered in class. ### Mid-Semester Reassurance Midway through the semester, I reassure students that there is usually a point where the program clicks for them. Up until that point, many feel frustrated or discouraged, but once they reach that plateau of learning, they often feel more comfortable and capable. ## Technical Limitations Students may face technical limitations due to the program's size and processing power requirements, especially during advanced operations like animation. It's essential for departments to consider additional computer resources or lab setups to help facilitate the learning process. I also advise students not to underestimate the time required for animation rendering; it often takes longer than anticipated. Lastly, we discuss the deceptive nature of the 3D mesh and the need for rigorous assessment of garment fit. ## Closing Remarks Okay, and I would like to introduce Christian Settle. Just a little backstory: I never really expected to be in the fashion industry at all. I spent a lot of time doing graphic design and some 3D rendering. I would make mock-ups of t-shirts and hoodies, thinking they were cool. Eventually, I realized I wanted to elevate my understanding of fashion, which led me to VCU. ### Learning at VCU Through my time there, I learned a lot about the fundamentals of fashion design. My senior year, I enrolled in the CLO3 class, which changed the way I thought about fashion design. The software allowed me to visualize ideas and provided unlimited potential for experimentation. I was passionate about sustainability, and the department emphasized this as well. I took a sustainability class that highlighted issues of overproduction and overconsumption. CLO 3D helped me slow down my design process without affecting deadlines. ### Post-Graduation Career Post-graduation, I started a career with CLO 3D, focusing on technical design.
